title: Handball
description: Team sport with two teams of seven players each
wiki_lead:
Handball (also known as team handball, European handball, Olympic handball, or indoor handball) is a team sport in which two teams of seven players each (six outcourt players and a goalkeeper) pass a ball using their hands with the aim of throwing it into the goal of the opposing team. A standard match consists of two periods of 30 minutes, and the team that scores more goals wins.
Modern handball is played on a court of 40 by 20 metres (131 by 66 ft), with a goal in the middle of each end. The goals are surrounded by a 6-metre (20 ft) zone where only the defending goalkeeper is allowed; goals must be scored by throwing the ball from outside the zone or while "diving" into it. The sport is usually played indoors, but outdoor variants exist in the forms of field handball, Czech handball (which were more common in the past) and beach handball. The game is fast and high-scoring: professional teams now typically score between 20 and 35 goals each, though lower scores were not uncommon until a few decades ago. Body contact is permitted for the defenders trying to stop the attackers from approaching the goal. No protective equipment is mandated, but players may wear soft protective bands, pads and mouth guards.
The modern set of rules was published in 1917 by Karl Schelenz, Max Heiser, and Erich Konigh, on 29 October in Berlin, which is seen as the date of birth of the sport. The rules have had several revisions since. The first official handball match was played in 1917 in Germany. Karl Schelenz modified the rules in 1919. The first international games were played (under these rules) with men in 1925 and with women in 1930, both between Germany and Austria.
Men's handball was first played at the Olympics in the 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin outdoors, and the next time at the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich indoors; handball has been an Olympic sport since then. Women's handball was added at the 1976 Summer Olympics.
The International Handball Federation was formed in 1946 and, as of 2016, has 197 member federations. The sport is most popular in Europe, and European countries have won all medals but one in the men's Olympic Games tournament since 1972 and men's world championships since 1938. In the women's world championships, only two non-European countries have won the world title - South Korea and Brazil - whilst only the former have also won an Olympic medal. The game also enjoys popularity in East Asia, North Africa and parts of South America.

Origins and development

Games similar to handball were played in Ancient Greece and are represented on amphorae and stone carvings. Although detailed textual reference is rare, there are numerous descriptions of ball games being played where players throw the ball to one another; sometimes this is done in order to avoid interception by a player on the opposing team. Such games were played widely and served as both a form of exercise and a social event.
There is evidence of ancient Roman women playing a version of handball called expulsim ludere. There are records of handball-like games in medieval France, and among the Inuit in Greenland, in the Middle Ages. By the 19th century, there existed similar games of håndbold from Denmark, házená in the Czech Republic, handbol in Ukraine, and torball in Germany.
The team handball game of today was codified at the end of the 19th century in northern Europe: primarily in Denmark, Germany, Norway, and Sweden. The first written set of team handball rules was published in 1906 by the Danish gym teacher, lieutenant and Olympic medalist Holger Nielsen from Ordrup grammar school, north of Copenhagen. grok_lead: Handball is a dynamic team sport played indoors between two teams of seven players eachâsix outfield players and one goalkeeperâwho pass and throw a spherical ball using their hands to score goals by propelling it past the opposing goalkeeper into a netted goal measuring 3 meters wide and 2 meters high. The game takes place on a rectangular court 40 meters long and 20 meters wide, with a 6-meter goal area restricted to the goalkeeper, and matches consist of two 30-minute halves separated by a 10- to 15-minute halftime break. Players may hold the ball for up to 3 seconds and take up to 3 steps while in possession, with dribbling permitted but limited to avoid double dribbles, emphasizing speed, agility, and physical contact within strict rules against holding, pushing, or dangerous play. The sport's modern origins trace back to late 19th-century Europe, with early forms resembling handball documented in ancient Rome and northern European games, but formalized rules first published in Denmark in 1906 and refined in Germany in 1917 for an 11-player outdoor version known as field handball. Indoor handball, the dominant format today, evolved in the 1910s in Denmark, Germany, and Sweden, leading to the founding of the International Handball Federation (IHF) in Copenhagen in 1946 to standardize and promote the game globally. Field handball debuted as an Olympic demonstration sport in 1936, while team handball (indoor) was introduced to the Summer Olympics in 1972 for men and 1976 for women, boosting its international profile. Handball encompasses several variants adapted for different environments and participants, including beach handball âplayed on sand with 4 players per team (3 outfield and 1 goalkeeper) in two 10-minute halves, officially recognized by the IHF in 1994 and featured in multi- sport events since 2013âand wheelchair handball, a four-a-side inclusive version for athletes with disabilities that follows modified indoor rules to ensure accessibility and fairness. The IHF, now comprising 209 national federations, governs the sport worldwide, organizing events like the Men's and Women's World Championships every two years and supporting regional bodies such as the European Handball Federation (EHF), founded in 1991, which oversees premier competitions including the EHF EURO and Champions League. With approximately 27 million registered players across 209 national federations, handball thrives at professional, amateur, and recreational levels, renowned for its high-intensity action, strategic passing, and athletic demands that combine elements of basketball, soccer, and rugby.
